summary: Overruled Swift v. Tyson and held that federal courts sitting in diversity must apply state law rather than a general federal common law. It is the foundation of the modern division of labor between federal and state courts.

Held that a state court has no personal jurisdiction over a non-resident who was not served within the state and did not consent, grounding the rule in Fourteenth Amendment due process. It set the territorial framework for personal jurisdiction later reworked in International Shoe.

case_name: Second Employers' Liability Cases (Mondou v. New York, N.H. & H.R. Co.)
summary: Upheld the Federal Employers' Liability Act as a valid exercise of the commerce power over railroad employment, superseding conflicting state law. It also held that state courts must hear federal claims created by the Act.

case_name: The Propeller Genesee Chief v. Fitzhugh
summary: Extended federal admiralty jurisdiction from tidal waters to all navigable waters, including the Great Lakes and inland rivers. It overruled the English tidewater rule and opened the interior of the country to admiralty law.

Held that the general maritime law applies in the United States only as adopted and modified by American law, and that no maritime lien arises for supplies furnished in a vessel's home port. It defined the relationship between federal maritime law and state law.

case_name: Liverpool & Great Western Steam Co. v. Phenix Insurance Co.
summary: Held that a common carrier cannot by contract exempt itself from liability for its own negligence, and that the validity of a bill of lading is governed by the law of the place where it was made. An insurer who paid the shipper was subrogated to the shipper's claim against the carrier.

Held that a corporation chartered in one state may make contracts and do business in another state as a matter of comity unless that state's law forbids it. It established the basic framework for interstate corporate activity.

Held that pledgees holding corporate stock as collateral were not liable as stockholders under a Missouri statute, and that federal courts may exercise independent judgment on state law when no state decision was settled before the rights accrued. It is a leading pre-Erie statement of federal deference to state courts.

Held that when several plaintiffs have separate and distinct claims, each claim must independently exceed the jurisdictional amount for Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction. It is a foundational amount-in-controversy case.

Held that sureties on a federal officer's bond are liable only for duties existing under the statutes in force when the bond was given, and that delay by government officers is not laches chargeable against the United States. It set early rules for government surety bonds.

Established judicial review, holding that the Supreme Court may declare an act of Congress unconstitutional. The Court found Marbury entitled to his commission but held the statute granting it original jurisdiction to issue mandamus invalid.

Held that the Supreme Court has appellate jurisdiction over state court decisions involving federal law, treaties, and the Constitution. It secured uniform interpretation of federal law across the states.
Held that the Supreme Court may review state criminal judgments that raise federal questions, even where the state is a party. On the merits it upheld Virginia's lottery conviction.

case_name: Osborn v. Bank of the United States
summary: Held that federal courts have jurisdiction over suits by the Bank of the United States because its federal charter is an ingredient of every case, and that state officers enforcing an unconstitutional tax may be enjoined notwithstanding the Eleventh Amendment. It is the root of modern federal-question and officer-suit doctrine.

Held that a state official enforcing an unconstitutional statute acts without state authority and may be enjoined by a federal court despite the Eleventh Amendment. It is the main route for federal suits against state officers.

Held that land reserved by the federal government for military purposes is withdrawn from the public domain and not subject to pre-emption claims, and that only a patent passes full title to public lands. It defined the limits of state law over federal land titles.

Held that new states enter the Union on an equal footing with the original states and therefore own the lands beneath their navigable waters. The United States could not convey such submerged lands after Alabama's admission.

Introduced the distinction between self-executing and non-self-executing treaties, holding that a treaty provision promising future ratification of land grants required an act of Congress before courts could enforce it. It governs how treaties operate as domestic law.

Held that compelling a person to produce private papers for use against him is an unreasonable search under the Fourth Amendment and compelled self-incrimination under the Fifth. It is the source of the constitutional protection of private papers and the exclusionary idea.

Held that the Fifth Amendment's double jeopardy protection was not then incorporated against the states, because only rights implicit in ordered liberty bind the states. The incorporation test it announced governed until Benton v. Maryland overruled it in 1969.

Held that evidence obtained by an unconstitutional search is inadmissible in state as well as federal courts, overruling Wolf v. Colorado. It applied the exclusionary rule to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.

Held that the Sixth Amendment requires states to provide counsel to indigent defendants in felony prosecutions, overruling Betts v. Brady. The right to counsel was declared fundamental to a fair trial.

Held that statements from custodial interrogation are inadmissible unless the suspect was warned of the right to remain silent and to counsel and validly waived those rights. It created the Miranda warning as a Fifth Amendment safeguard.

Held that the Fourth Amendment protects people rather than places, so warrantless electronic eavesdropping on a phone booth was an unconstitutional search. It overruled Olmstead's trespass test and produced the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy standard.

Held that the Free Exercise Clause applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment and struck down a licensing scheme that let officials judge whether a cause was religious. It is the starting point of modern free exercise doctrine.

name_key: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan
case_name: New York Times Co. v. Sullivan
summary: Held that a public official cannot recover for defamation about official conduct without proving actual malice, meaning knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth. It constitutionalized libel law under the First Amendment.

Held that a facially neutral laundry ordinance enforced only against Chinese operators violated the Equal Protection Clause, which protects all persons within the jurisdiction, not only citizens. It established that discriminatory administration of a law is unconstitutional.

Upheld the TVA's contract to sell power from Wilson Dam as within federal authority. Justice Brandeis's concurrence set out the seven rules of constitutional avoidance that courts still cite when declining to reach constitutional questions.

case_name: NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp.
summary: Upheld the National Labor Relations Act, holding that Congress may regulate intrastate activities such as manufacturing labor relations that substantially affect interstate commerce. It marked the Court's shift away from striking down New Deal legislation.

case_name: United States v. Socony-Vacuum Oil Co.
summary: Held that agreements to fix or stabilize prices in interstate commerce are illegal per se under the Sherman Act, regardless of the reasonableness of the prices or the evils they were meant to cure. It is the leading per se price-fixing case.

case_name: Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States
summary: Held that Standard Oil was an illegal monopoly under the Sherman Act and ordered its dissolution. The opinion adopted the rule of reason, under which only unreasonable restraints of trade are prohibited.

Held that the meatpackers' combination to control livestock prices violated the Sherman Act because local stockyard transactions were part of a continuous stream of interstate commerce. It originated the stream-of-commerce doctrine.

Held a patent for preserving fish and meat by freezing void for lack of novelty, because applying a known process to a new subject is not invention. It is an early statement of the novelty requirement in patent law.

Held that Congress has implied power under the Necessary and Proper Clause to charter a national bank and that states may not tax federal instrumentalities. It established federal supremacy and the broad reading of congressional power.

Held that the Commerce Clause gives Congress power over interstate navigation, so a federal coasting license overrode New York's steamboat monopoly. It is the foundational broad reading of the commerce power.

Upheld Louisiana's slaughterhouse monopoly and read the Privileges or Immunities Clause to protect only rights of national, not state, citizenship. It sharply narrowed that clause and pushed later civil rights litigation toward due process and equal protection.

Upheld Illinois's maximum rates for grain elevators, holding that property affected with a public interest may be regulated by the state. It is the source of the public-interest doctrine in economic regulation.

Held that a corporate charter does not impliedly exempt the corporation from state taxation, so a later tax did not impair the obligation of contract. It established that surrenders of the taxing power must be express.

Struck down Nebraska's railroad rate schedule as confiscatory, holding that regulated rates must allow a fair return on the fair value of the property. The fair-value rule governed utility regulation until FPC v. Hope Natural Gas in 1944.

Held that a state may set intrastate railroad rates even if they incidentally affect interstate commerce, absent federal action. It also refined the fair-value method for judging whether rates are confiscatory.

case_name: Murray's Lessee v. Hoboken Land & Improvement Co.
summary: Upheld a Treasury distress warrant against a defaulting customs collector, holding that due process means the settled usages of English and American law rather than whatever process Congress chooses. It was the Court's first extended interpretation of the Due Process Clause.

case_name: Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad Co. v. Chicago
summary: Held that the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause requires states to pay just compensation when taking private property, though a nominal award for a street crossing was upheld on the facts. It was the first incorporation of a Bill of Rights guarantee against the states.

case_name: Monongahela Navigation Co. v. United States
summary: Held that when the United States condemns a lock and dam it must compensate the owner for the franchise to collect tolls as well as the physical property. It is a leading statement that just compensation means a full equivalent for everything taken.

Refused to issue mandamus against a district judge over an attorney's fee award, holding that extraordinary writs are reserved for cases where appeal is clearly inadequate. It is routinely cited when the Court declines mandamus.

Held that settling a capital defendant's trial transcript in proceedings from which he and his counsel were excluded violated procedural due process. The Court required a new settlement of the record before Chessman's appeal could stand.

Held that whether an instrument is subject to stamp duty depends on its form and face, not on the purpose for which it was issued, so drafts designed to avoid the tax were lawful. It is an early authority that arranging affairs to minimize tax is not fraud.

Held that shells cleaned and polished for sale remained unmanufactured shells for tariff purposes because they kept their original form and character. Its definition of manufacture is still cited, including in Diamond v. Chakrabarty.
